explore_learn_subtitle: The basics, without the fuss, so you can enjoy every glass.
learn_body_summary: How heavy and rich the wine feels in your mouth.
learn_body_intro: Body is the sense of "weight" a wine leaves in your mouth. Think of the difference between skim milk, whole milk and cream: light, medium and full-bodied wines feel a lot like that.
learn_body_point_1: Light: fresh and easy to drink, like many whites, rosés and Pinot Noir.
learn_body_point_2: Medium: balanced and versatile, like Merlot and many Italian reds.
learn_body_point_3: Full: dense and bold, like Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec and Syrah.
learn_body_point_4: More alcohol, sugar and tannins usually make a wine feel fuller.
learn_body_tip: Taste a light wine and a full-bodied one side by side: the difference becomes obvious.
learn_acidity_summary: The freshness that makes your mouth water.
learn_acidity_intro: Acidity is what makes a wine taste fresh and lively. If your mouth starts watering after a sip, that's acidity at work.
learn_acidity_point_1: High acidity: vibrant, refreshing wines like Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and sparkling wines.
learn_acidity_point_2: Low acidity: softer, rounder wines; with too little, a wine can taste "flat".
learn_acidity_point_3: Cool regions usually make crisper wines; warm regions, riper and softer ones.
learn_acidity_point_4: Acidity helps wine pair with food, especially fatty dishes or tomato sauces.
learn_acidity_tip: Compare a Sauvignon Blanc with an oaked Chardonnay and notice which one makes your mouth water more.
learn_tannins_summary: That drying feeling red wines leave in your mouth.
learn_tannins_intro: Tannins come from grape skins and seeds, and also from oak barrels. They make your mouth feel dry and rough, like strong black tea or an unripe banana.
learn_tannins_point_1: They show up mostly in reds, which ferment together with the skins.
learn_tannins_point_2: High tannins: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat and Nebbiolo.
learn_tannins_point_3: Low tannins: Pinot Noir, Gamay and most whites and rosés.
learn_tannins_point_4: With time in the bottle, tannins become softer and silkier.
learn_tannins_point_5: Protein and fat, like red meat and aged cheeses, soften tannins.
learn_tannins_tip: Tannin isn't a flaw, it's structure. If it bothers you, drink the wine with food.
learn_types_summary: Red, white, rosé, sparkling and dessert.
learn_types_intro: Most wines fit into five big styles. The color comes from how long the juice stays in contact with the grape skins.
learn_types_point_1: Red: red grapes fermented with their skins, which add color and tannins.
learn_types_point_2: White: usually white grapes, with no skin contact; lighter and more refreshing.
learn_types_point_3: Rosé: red grapes with only brief skin contact, just enough for the pink color.
learn_types_point_4: Sparkling: bubbles from a second fermentation, like Champagne, Prosecco and Cava.
learn_types_point_5: Dessert and fortified: sweet wines and/or wines with added alcohol, like Port, Moscato and Sauternes.
learn_types_tip: Serve whites, rosés and sparkling wines well chilled (6–10 °C) and reds slightly below room temperature (14–18 °C).
learn_pairing_summary: Simple rules for matching wine and food.
learn_pairing_intro: Pairing means making the wine and the food bring out the best in each other. There are no strict rules, but a few principles help a lot.
learn_pairing_point_1: Match weight with weight: light dishes call for light wines; rich dishes call for full-bodied wines.
learn_pairing_point_2: Red and fatty meats go well with tannic reds like Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec.
learn_pairing_point_3: Fish, seafood and salads go well with crisp whites and sparkling wines.
learn_pairing_point_4: With desserts, the wine should be at least as sweet as the dish.
learn_pairing_point_5: Local dishes usually pair well with wines from the same region.
learn_pairing_tip: When in doubt, a brut sparkling wine goes well with everything from snacks to light dishes.
learn_vintage_summary: The year the grapes were harvested.
learn_vintage_intro: The vintage is the year the grapes were harvested, the number shown on the label. That year's weather influences how the wine tastes.
learn_vintage_point_1: Years with good weather tend to produce more balanced wines with better aging potential.
learn_vintage_point_2: Most wines are made to be enjoyed young, within 2 or 3 years.
learn_vintage_point_3: Only some wines improve for decades, usually well-structured reds and some sweet wines.
learn_vintage_point_4: Non-vintage wines, like many sparkling wines, blend grapes from different years to keep a consistent style.
learn_vintage_tip: Store bottles on their side, away from light and heat, at a steady temperature.
learn_grapes_summary: Get to know the most popular varieties.
learn_grapes_intro: Each grape variety has its own personality. Knowing a few helps you pick wines that suit your taste.
learn_grapes_point_1: Cabernet Sauvignon: full-bodied, tannic red with notes of blackcurrant, plum and bell pepper.
learn_grapes_point_2: Merlot: soft, fruity red with notes of plum and chocolate; great for beginners.
learn_grapes_point_3: Malbec: intense, velvety red, Argentina's star, with notes of blackberry and violet.
learn_grapes_point_4: Pinot Noir: light, elegant red with notes of cherry and strawberry.
learn_grapes_point_5: Chardonnay: versatile white, from crisp and citrusy to creamy and buttery when aged in oak.
learn_grapes_point_6: Sauvignon Blanc: aromatic, very fresh white with notes of passion fruit, lime and grass.
learn_grapes_tip: Liked a wine? Note the grape on the label: it's the easiest way to find similar ones.
learn_tip_1: Hold your glass by the stem so your hand doesn't warm the wine.
learn_tip_2: Swirl the wine in your glass before smelling it: it helps release the aromas.
learn_tip_3: Once opened, wine keeps for 2 to 5 days in the fridge, tightly closed.
learn_tip_4: For sparkling wines, "brut" means dry; "demi-sec" and "doux" are sweeter.
learn_tip_5: Mouth feels dry after a sip of red? Those are the tannins.
learn_tip_6: Wines with good acidity go well with fatty foods: each balances the other.
learn_tip_7: Light reds like Pinot Noir are great slightly chilled.
learn_tip_8: The year on the label is the vintage: the year the grapes were harvested.
learn_tip_9: Spicy food? Go for wines with less alcohol and a touch of sweetness, like a Riesling.
learn_tip_10: Merlot is a great grape to start with reds: soft and fruity.
learn_tip_11: Rate the wines you taste: your ratings help Vinum recommend better.
